title: Website Migration SEO: How to Avoid Expensive Mistakes
summary: Website migration SEO advice from Webflow partners: what to keep, how to map 301 redirects, and what to check after launch day.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


In 2026, the most expensive website migration mistakes usually happen at the start and the end of the project. Before the move, decide what is worth keeping, cut what is not performing, and map a 301 redirect for every URL that changes. That includes the URLs your login, signup, and payment tools depend on. After the move, keep measuring and keep publishing. Recheck your redirects a few weeks later, and leave with a design system so the new site does not slowly turn back into the old one.


On October 27, 2026,[Mark Williams](https://www.linkedin.com/in/msijuadewilliams/) of[NUUX Design Studios](https://www.nuuxstudios.com/) asked a group of Webflow partners a simple question on LinkedIn: what is the most expensive mistake you have seen a company make during a replatform? Four partners answered. Developers, SEO specialists, and agency founders then continued the conversation in the comments, adding the checks they rely on.


[Jakob Kastelic](https://www.linkedin.com/in/leon-jakob-kastelic-089b8b164/) of Flowout read the four answers together and noticed that they line up like a timeline. Two are about deciding what to bring with you. The other two are about what happens once the site is live. As he put it, most teams “nail the middle and skip both ends.”


Here is what the community said:


## **Decide What Deserves to Make the Trip**


Jakob’s answer was blunt: “Migrating junk costs exactly as much as migrating content that works.”


He sees teams treat a migration as a visual rebuild, with the same pages and the same structure on a nicer platform. They pay full price to move content nobody reads. He has seen clients cut around 40 percent of their pages after looking at what was not performing. They then redirect those URLs to relevant pages and build templates before migrating anything.


Two cautions came up in the comments.


Do not judge a page by traffic alone.[Roman Sadowski](https://www.linkedin.com/in/roman-sadowski-3a2545187/) of Rankdough pointed out that a page with few visits can still carry the links other sites use to point to you. Before you cut a page, check the backlinks.


Do not add pages in the middle of the move.[Duncan Hamra](https://www.linkedin.com/in/duncanhamra/) , co-founder of Memberstack, warned that adding new pages during a migration is how a one month project turns into a six month project. Finish the move first, then build.


## **Start With What Is Already Working**


Mark Williams, who started the conversation, has a simple rule for any replatform: before you rebuild anything, find out what is already working and why. He breaks that into three checks:


- Which pages drive traffic today. Pull the numbers from Google Analytics and Google Search Console before anyone touches the design. These are the pages you cannot afford to lose.
- The SEO and AEO strategy behind them. A page ranks in Google or gets cited by AI answer engines for a reason, such as the questions it answers or the way it is structured. If the new version drops what made the old one work, the results go with it.
- The URLs and redirects. A migration feels like a fresh start, so everything gets rebuilt and renamed at once. If your blog already lives at a short, clear URL, keep it. If you do change a URL, that page needs a proper redirect, and that is the step that gets skipped. Then the new site goes live, looks great, and traffic drops.


## **Protect the Pages That Already Rank**


[Youssef Rashad AbdelFattah](https://www.linkedin.com/in/yabdelfattah1/) of Kaii Lab named the mistake that came up more than any other: “The most expensive mistake during a replatform is not performing 301 redirects and losing organic traffic from already ranking pages.”


Commenters shared the process they use to avoid that:


Export the full list of old URLs from your old sitemap and Google Search Console.


Map each old URL to its new page in a spreadsheet.


Test the redirects on staging with pages that get real traffic, not just the homepage.[Mudasir Lal](https://www.linkedin.com/in/mudasir-lal-80740a233/) pointed out that a redirect can work and still send people to the wrong content.


After launch, run that exact list through a crawler.[Swadhin Khan Mohammad Nakib](https://www.linkedin.com/in/ssswadhin/) of DianaHost recommends checking that each old URL returns a single 301 that goes straight to a working page. Redirect chains and quiet 404 errors are easy to miss when you only click through the main pages.


Keep the list. Swadhin also recommends checking it again a few weeks later, because redirects often break during the first round of fixes after launch.


Roman added why this matters beyond traffic. If you skip the redirect, the links pointing at the old page stop helping the new one.


## **Remember the URLs Your Tools Depend On**


The team at Memberstack raised a point that the SEO side of the conversation did not cover: Google is not the only thing that knows your URLs. Your login and signup flows, your payment success pages, and the links in your automated welcome emails all point to specific pages. These can break even when your SEO redirects are perfect.


This matters most for membership sites. Usually nobody notices until after launch, when a new member emails support to say something is broken. Before you go live, check the redirect settings in your membership tool, the success and cancel pages in your payment provider, and every link in your automated emails.


## **Do Not Treat Launch Day as the Finish Line**


[Alex Olivero](https://www.linkedin.com/in/alexxolivero/) of Curio Digital described the mistake that happens after the move: “The most expensive mistake I see is treating launch day as the finish line. No new content, nobody looking at analytics, no testing.”


Mark explored a related problem in another post. Many teams measure their campaigns, but nobody measures the website that sits between the click and the sale. In one case, a client was running ChatGPT ads with a large monthly budget, and the conversion event was simply traffic. Nobody could tell whether the page people landed on did anything. Often Google Analytics gets set up and that is where it stops.


The commenters offered a few fixes:


Add a tool that shows behavior, not just visits. Mark and Alex both recommend Microsoft Clarity, which is free and shows where people drop off.


Give someone ownership of the website.[Umair Suleman](https://www.linkedin.com/in/umair-suleman/) of Useryze said the website is often owned by “kind of nobody.” Design owns how it looks and marketing owns what sends people there. He suggests giving one person both the click to lead number and the authority to change the page.


Measure the real conversion. Memberstack pointed out that for a membership site, the real conversion is a member signing up or choosing a paid plan, not a visit to the pricing page. Many sites have great traffic and lose people right at the signup form, and nobody notices because the ad numbers look fine.


Compare your top landing pages a few weeks after launch to catch anything that slipped through.


## **Leave With a Design System**


[Pavel Karpisek](https://www.linkedin.com/in/pkarpisek/) of Karpi Studio called this the most expensive thing he sees today: “Companies replatform and walk away without a design system.”


This ties back to why many teams replatform in the first place. Jakob noted that the problem teams are trying to escape is usually that marketing needs a developer to ship anything. Without a design system of reusable components and clear rules, the new site slowly drifts and the old problem comes back. A design system lets your team build new pages without starting from scratch every time.


## A Quick Website Migration Checklist


1. Audit which pages drive traffic, conversions, and backlinks, and note the SEO and AEO strategy behind each one, before you move anything.
2. Cut or consolidate pages that are not performing, and redirect them to relevant content.
3. Hold off on new pages until the migration is finished.
4. Map every changed URL to a 301 redirect, and test it on staging with real traffic pages.
5. Check login, signup, payment, and email links, not just SEO pages.
6. Crawl your full list of old URLs after launch, then crawl it again a few weeks later.
7. Measure what happens on the site, not just how many people arrive.
8. Leave with a design system your team can build on.


## Final Thoughts


A replatform is as much about what you leave behind as what you bring with you, and the work does not end when the new site goes live. Thank you to Mark Williams and to Youssef, Jakob, Alex, and Pavel for sharing their experience, and to everyone who added to the conversation in the comments.


If your replatform includes member logins, gated content, or paid plans, Memberstack can help you rebuild those flows on Webflow without starting over. Make sure your membership URLs are on your redirect checklist from day one.


## Frequently Asked Questions


Q. What does replatforming a website mean?Replatforming means moving your website from one platform to another, for example, leaving WordPress and going to Webflow. Your content, URLs, and integrations all have to come with you or be deliberately left behind.


Q. Does a website redesign or migration hurt SEO?


It can, but it does not have to. Traffic usually drops when URLs change without 301 redirects, or when pages that already rank are rebuilt without the content and structure that made them work. Before you move, check which pages drive traffic, keep the SEO and AEO strategy behind them, and map a redirect for every URL that changes.


Q. What is the most common replatforming mistake?The mistake that came up most in this discussion was skipping 301 redirects on pages that already rank. That causes lost organic traffic and lost value from backlinks.


Q. How do I decide which pages to keep during a migration?Look at traffic, conversions, and backlinks together. A page with low traffic may still have valuable links pointing to it. Pages that do poorly on all three are candidates to cut and redirect.


Q. How long after launch should I recheck redirects?Commenters recommend running your full list of old URLs through a crawler right after launch and again a few weeks later, since redirects often break during the first round of fixes.


Q. What should I track after a replatform?Track the actions that matter to your business, such as signups, paid plans, or leads, not just visits. A tool like Microsoft Clarity can show you where visitors drop off.
